Rainy days in London are actually a great excuse to duck indoors into some of its best spots. A few ideas that fit walking, food, and exploring:

1. British Museum – Free entry and enormous, so you can easily spend half a day here. The Rosetta Stone and Egyptian galleries are the highlights, and there's a covered courtyard if you need a coffee break.
2. Borough Market – A short walk from London Bridge, this covered food market is great for grazing lunch, trying local produce, and people-watching under a roof.
3. Tate Modern – A world-class modern art museum in a converted power station on the South Bank, with free general admission. The building alone is worth the visit.
4. Afternoon tea – A very London way to spend a rainy afternoon. Somewhere like Fortnum & Mason or a nice hotel gives you a couple of relaxed hours out of the weather with excellent food.
5. A West End show – Book a matinee or evening performance. It's one of the best theatre scenes in the world and a perfect way to end a rainy day of walking.

Most of these sit near good walking routes (South Bank, Bloomsbury, Covent Garden), so if the rain lets up even briefly you can combine them with exploring on foot.

A few genuinely strange corners of music worth digging into:

1. Vaporwave – Slowed-down, pitch-shifted samples of 80s/90s elevator music and corporate soft rock, wrapped in a nostalgic, slightly eerie internet aesthetic. Think Floral Shoppe by Macintosh Plus.
2. Dungeon synth – Lo-fi, atmospheric synthesizer music meant to evoke medieval fantasy settings, castles, and forests. It grew out of the black metal scene as a side-project genre.
3. Breakcore – Extremely fast, chopped-up breakbeats mashed together with elements of jungle, gabber, and noise. Chaotic and abrasive by design.
4. Drone doom – Metal stripped down to sustained, glacially slow chords, sometimes a single riff repeated for 20+ minutes. Sunn O))) is the reference point.
5. Chiptune – Music made using the sound chips of old video game consoles and computers, still actively produced today as its own genre rather than just nostalgia.
6. Gqom – A dark, minimal, percussion-heavy strain of house music that emerged from Durban, South Africa in the early 2010s.

If any of these catch your interest, a good next step is searching the genre name plus "essentials" or "starter pack" on YouTube or a streaming service — most have small but dedicated communities that curate entry points.

That "blah" feeling is usually your body flagging that a few basics have slipped. Some habits worth trying:

1. Get outside for at least 10–15 minutes of daylight, ideally in the morning — it helps reset your circadian rhythm and mood.
2. Move your body, even just a walk. You don't need a workout, just consistent movement.
3. Drink water first thing and stay ahead of dehydration through the day — low-grade dehydration alone can make you feel sluggish and foggy.
4. Eat real meals at regular times instead of grazing or skipping — blood sugar swings can feel a lot like just feeling "off."
5. Prioritize sleep, both duration and consistency. Going to bed and waking up around the same time matters as much as total hours.
6. Cut back on scrolling, especially first thing in the morning and right before bed.
7. Do one small task you've been avoiding — a messy inbox or pile of dishes has a way of quietly weighing on mood.
8. Spend a little time with people you like, even a short call. Isolation compounds the blah feeling.
9. Step outside your routine with something you enjoy — reading, music, a hobby — even for 20 minutes.
10. Check in on your caffeine and alcohol intake, since both can mess with sleep and energy without you noticing.

None of these are dramatic changes, but stacking a few of them for a week tends to move the needle more than any single one.

A few US suburbs that fit that brief — decent size, low crime, upscale feel with good shopping and newer apartment options:

1. Alpharetta, Georgia (suburb of Atlanta) – Around 68,000 people, consistently ranks as one of the safer cities in Georgia, and has Avalon, a large upscale mixed-use development with shopping, dining, and modern apartments.
2. Plano, Texas (suburb of Dallas) – Around 290,000 people, so bigger, but still feels suburban. Low crime for its size, strong schools, and Legacy West is a polished shopping and residential district with a lot of newer high-end apartments.
3. Naperville, Illinois (suburb of Chicago) – Around 149,000 people, regularly ranks among the safest and best places to live in the country, with a walkable downtown, riverwalk, and upscale shopping.
4. Bellevue, Washington (suburb of Seattle) – Around 150,000 people, very low crime, and has The Bravern and other high-end retail alongside a growing skyline of newer luxury apartment towers.
5. Short Hills, New Jersey (suburb of NYC, part of Millburn Township) – Smaller, around 14,000 people, but very affluent, low crime, and home to The Mall at Short Hills, one of the more upscale shopping centers on the East Coast.

Alpharetta and Naperville probably fit your brief most closely — both are big enough to feel established and safe, and built around newer upscale development rather than an older downtown core.

Here's a minimal example using Pygame:

```python
import pygame

pygame.init()

# Window setup
WIDTH, HEIGHT = 800, 600
screen = pygame.display.set_mode((WIDTH, HEIGHT))
pygame.display.set_caption("My First Game")
clock = pygame.time.Clock()

# Player setup
player_size = 50
player_x, player_y = WIDTH // 2, HEIGHT // 2
player_speed = 5

running = True
while running:
    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            running = False

    # Handle held-down keys for movement
    keys = pygame.key.get_pressed()
    if keys[pygame.K_LEFT]:
        player_x -= player_speed
    if keys[pygame.K_RIGHT]:
        player_x += player_speed
    if keys[pygame.K_UP]:
        player_y -= player_speed
    if keys[pygame.K_DOWN]:
        player_y += player_speed

    # Draw everything
    screen.fill((30, 30, 30))  # background color
    pygame.draw.rect(screen, (0, 200, 255), (player_x, player_y, player_size, player_size))

    pygame.display.flip()
    clock.tick(60)  # cap at 60 FPS

pygame.quit()
```

This opens an 800x600 window with a blue square you can move around using the arrow keys. A few next steps once this feels good:

- Swap the rectangle for a sprite image with `pygame.image.load("player.png")`.
- Use `pygame.sprite.Sprite` and `pygame.sprite.Group` once you have more than one object on screen — it makes collision detection much easier.
- Add boundary checks so the player can't walk off the edge of the window.

Make sure you install Pygame first with `pip install pygame`.

This is Tailwind CSS using the `@apply` directive, which lets you bundle a group of utility classes into a single custom class name (typically defined inside a `@layer components` block).

`.action-panel`:
- `fixed` — positioned relative to the viewport, so it stays in place when the page scrolls
- `left-0` — pinned to the left edge
- `flex flex-col` — a flex container laying its children out vertically
- `top-72` — positioned 18rem from the top
- `space-y-2` — adds vertical spacing (0.5rem) between each child element

`.action-button`:
- `bg-white` — white background
- `relative` — positioned relative to its normal position (needed for `top-2` to have an effect)
- `top-2` — nudged down 0.5rem from where it would normally sit
- `py-2 px-6` — vertical padding of 0.5rem and horizontal padding of 1.5rem
- `text-center` — centers the text inside the button

So in practice: `.action-panel` is a fixed vertical strip of buttons pinned to the left side of the screen, roughly a third of the way down, and `.action-button` styles each individual button inside it as a white, padded, centered pill nudged slightly down from its default position.

Most people picture Egypt when they hear the word "pyramid," but the largest pyramid by volume in the world is actually in Cholula, Mexico. Known as Tlachihualtepetl, or the Great Pyramid of Cholula, it stands about 66 meters (217 feet) tall with a base measuring roughly 450 by 450 meters, giving it a far greater total volume than the Great Pyramid of Giza. Construction happened in stages over centuries, with work carried out between around 300 BCE and 700 CE. A temple dedicated to Quetzalcoatl, the god of learning and wind, once sat atop the structure, but it was abandoned by the 8th or 9th century AD and gradually became overgrown with vegetation, disguising it as a natural hill. When Spanish conquistadors arrived in 1521, they didn't recognize it as a pyramid at all and built a church on the summit — a church that still stands there today. The true nature of the structure wasn't rediscovered until the 1930s, when erosion and archaeological excavation began revealing tunnels, altars, and murals inside. It remains a major tourist site and a striking example of how much history can hide in plain sight.

Dale Chihuly is an American glass artist widely credited with turning glassblowing into a recognized fine art form rather than just a craft or decorative technique. He's known for large-scale, brightly colored, often organic-looking glass installations — chandeliers, sculptural forms, and site-specific pieces installed in places like botanical gardens, museums, and public spaces around the world. Some of his most famous work includes pieces installed in the canals of Venice, Jerusalem's Old City, and the ceiling of the Bellagio hotel in Las Vegas. He runs a large studio that supports his ambitious, often massive-scale projects, since a lot of his later work is produced collaboratively with skilled glassblowing teams rather than by his hands alone.

Peanut butter's invention doesn't trace to a single person, despite the popular myth that credits George Washington Carver. A few key contributors:

- Marcellus Gilmore Edson, a Canadian, patented a process for making peanut paste in 1884, generally considered the earliest precursor to what we'd call peanut butter.
- John Harvey Kellogg (yes, of cereal fame) patented his own process for making nut butter from raw peanuts in the 1890s, initially promoting it as a protein source for patients who had trouble chewing solid food.
- Ambrose Straub later developed a peanut-butter-making machine, which helped it scale into a mass-market product.
- George Washington Carver didn't invent peanut butter, but his extensive research into peanut agriculture and its many applications helped drive demand for peanuts as a crop, which indirectly supported the growth of the peanut butter industry.

So it was more of an incremental invention across several people over a couple of decades than a single "aha" moment.

John Jacob Astor was a German-American businessman generally regarded as the first multi-millionaire in the United States. He made his fortune primarily through the fur trade — founding the American Fur Company in 1808 and the Pacific Fur Company in 1810 — and later expanded heavily into Manhattan real estate, which became an even larger source of his wealth over time. By the time of his death in 1848, he was the wealthiest person in the United States, and even adjusted for inflation, he remains one of the richest Americans in history. The Astor family went on to become one of the most prominent families in American history, with descendants involved in real estate, politics, and philanthropy for generations, including John Jacob Astor IV, who died on the Titanic.

Dear friend,

I have to tell you about how wild those first years on my own really were. Back in '76 and '77, I was scraping together income wherever I could find it — game shows, variety specials, you name it: Hollywood Squares, Donny & Marie, The Sonny & Cher Show, even The Brady Bunch Hour. Once I left Ike, the lawsuits started piling up over all the gigs we'd had to cancel, and I was drowning in debt. Mike Stewart over at United Artists was kind enough to front me the money to get back on the road and start paying it off.

By '77 I'd reinvented myself a bit — Bob Mackie designed some incredible new costumes for me, and I felt sexier and more confident than I had in years. I headlined cabaret shows at Caesars Palace, played smaller venues around the country, and even took my first solo tour to Australia.

The next year I put out Rough, my third solo album, and then Love Explosion in '79, where I dipped a toe into disco. Neither one really caught on, and United Artists and I parted ways after that. Still, I kept performing and headlined another tour regardless.

Then in '79, an Australian manager named Roger Davies caught my show at the Fairmont in San Francisco and offered to manage me — that turned out to be one of the best things that happened to me. I worked in Italy on a TV show called Luna Park, and later that year did a tour of South Africa that I've come to regret, honestly. I didn't understand the politics of apartheid the way I should have at the time.

Things really started turning around in October '81, when Rod Stewart caught my show at the Ritz in New York and invited me to perform with him on Saturday Night Live. A month later I was opening for the Rolling Stones on their American tour. The next year brought more good luck — a hit in the Netherlands with "Shame, Shame, Shame," and my cover of "Ball of Confusion" took off in European dance clubs. I even got to shoot a music video for it that aired on this new channel called MTV — I was one of the first Black American artists to get airtime there. And I closed out the year with a guest spot on Chuck Berry's TV special. It was a whirlwind, but it set the stage for everything that came after.

Love always

I used to think of jealousy as something that only showed up in romantic relationships — like when I couldn't stand the thought of my boyfriend talking to other women, or when I'd feel a pang seeing my ex post pictures with someone new online. But I've noticed it creeping into almost every relationship in my life, not just romantic ones. I feel it with my sister when I sense our parents paying more attention to her, and I feel it at work when a coworker seems to be winning over our boss more than I am.

It's a painful feeling to sit with, honestly. But I've come to see it differently after reading what evolutionary psychologists say about it — that jealousy isn't something I should suppress, but something I should actually listen to. It's like an internal alarm telling me a relationship I care about might be at risk, and that I need to do something to protect it. In that sense, I've started to think of jealousy less as a flaw in me and more as a signal that's actually trying to help me hold on to the people and bonds that matter.

1. Q: At what age range are people usually diagnosed with schizophrenia?
A: Between 16 and 30 years old.

2. Q: True or False — schizophrenia is common in young children.
A: False. It's rare in younger children.

3. Q: What are the three main categories of schizophrenia symptoms?
A: Psychotic, negative, and cognitive.

4. Q: Which of the following is a psychotic symptom?
a) Low energy b) Hallucinations c) Trouble concentrating d) Withdrawal
A: b) Hallucinations

5. Q: What is a delusion?
A: A strong, false belief that seems irrational to others, such as believing the TV is sending secret messages.

6. Q: Name two examples of negative symptoms.
A: Any two of: loss of motivation, reduced interest/pleasure in activities, social withdrawal, flat or dull affect, low energy.

7. Q: What rare condition involves a person stopping movement or speech for a period of time?
A: Catatonia.

8. Q: What kind of symptoms include problems with attention, concentration, and memory?
A: Cognitive symptoms.

9. Q: Why are negative symptoms sometimes misdiagnosed?
A: Because they can resemble symptoms of depression or other mental illnesses.

10. Q: According to the CDC, how can schizophrenia affect COVID-19 risk?
A: People with schizophrenia, along with certain other mental disorders, are more likely to become severely ill from COVID-19.

After WWII, states set their own daylight saving dates, which caused scheduling headaches for railroads. Congress standardized the dates nationally with the Uniform Time Act of 1966, later extended in 2007 to run from mid-March to early November. States can still opt out entirely — Arizona, Hawaii, and several U.S. territories stick to permanent standard time. Now momentum is building for change more broadly: more states are pushing legislation for either permanent standard or permanent daylight time, and the Senate even passed the Sunshine Protection Act in 2022 to make daylight saving permanent nationwide, though it stalled in the House. It's ultimately up to lawmakers whether the twice-yearly clock changes end, and which permanent time wins out.
